content:
Hi everyone, I’ve been looking at the Scientific Computing in Lean project:

https://lecopivo.github.io/scientific-computing-lean/

I’m interested in formalization related to scientific computing, especially PDEs / finite elements / numerical analysis. The project currently looks quite sparse, so I was wondering whether it is still being actively maintained.

If not, are there any other active Lean projects in this direction that you would recommend?

Thanks!

I'm not really developing nor maintaining the library right now and I'm not planning to resume anytime soon. Also it is not really formalization project anyway, I was trying to build library to actually do scientific computing in Lean.

Thanks a lot for the clarification — I really appreciate the reply.

That is very helpful to know. In that case, may I also ask whether you would recommend building on this library if the goal is formal verification for scientific computing, rather than doing scientific computing directly in Lean?

I’m mainly interested in formalizing things related to PDEs / finite elements / numerical analysis, so I’d be very interested to hear your perspective.

Tomas Skrivan said:

I'm not really developing nor maintaining the library right now and I'm not planning to resume anytime soon. Also it is not really formalization project anyway, I was trying to build library to actually do scientific computing in Lean.

Thanks a lot for the clarification — I really appreciate the reply.

That is very helpful to know. In that case, may I also ask whether you would recommend building on this library if the goal is formal verification for scientific computing, rather than doing scientific computing directly in Lean?

I’m mainly interested in formalizing things related to PDEs / finite elements / numerical analysis, so I’d be very interested to hear your perspective.

Fwiw, you can do formal verification on this library upto a point, since most algorithms are already defined for real numbers. I made a tiny PR to this library two years ago on newton's method. I think you can verify that in-principle.

I think the library won't give you much as I have spent the most time/effort on generic array interface and automatic differentiation. For formalization you will likely use Fin n -> Real for arrays anyway and I doubt that you will compute any complicated derivatives. I think your best bet is to just build on top of mathlib and just start with undergraduate numerical analysis. Basic interpolation, quadrature, ode time stepping methods. I think all of this is still missing in mathlib.
